blocks.text: Verdant Health Advisory LLC

We are a small healthcare advisory firm, and we spend our working lives in the part of this industry that rarely reaches the trade press: the plain question of which service lines actually earn their keep, whether a physician's compensation would survive a fair-market-value review, and where a revenue cycle is quietly losing money that everyone had assumed was arriving. Clients tend to find their way to us when one of those questions has become uncomfortable enough that it needs an answer they can defend rather than one that merely reassures, and that is the kind of work the firm was built for.
The register we write in

A great deal of what we produce is read by a general counsel before anyone acts on it, and we have learned to draft accordingly. What that means, in practice, is that we do not assert a conclusion the underlying analysis will not carry, and that we treat the language of fair market value as something to be used with care rather than as ornament. Our findings lead, our recommendations follow and are labelled as recommendations, and the line between the two is one we are unwilling to blur even in the moments when a client would plainly find the blurred version more comforting.
The questions clients bring us

Service line economics are the most common reason a health system calls. A hospital knows its total margin a good deal better than it knows the margin of any single department, and the patient work of separating the two, with the shared costs allocated in a way a skeptic would accept, is a large part of what we do. We present it findings first, with the recommendations set apart and identified as such, because the people who have to act on our work are entitled to see the evidence before they see our opinion of it.

Physician compensation is the second question, and it is the most sensitive of them. When a group asks whether an arrangement it has already entered into, or one it is only contemplating, sits within fair market value, the answer carries consequences that reach well beyond the spreadsheet, and we write those engagements knowing that counsel will weigh every qualifying clause. We say what the data support, we say plainly where the support runs out, and we have never regarded the sentence "the evidence does not reach that far" as a failure of the analysis.

The third question is the revenue cycle, where the trouble is rarely one dramatic leak and far more often a collection of small ones that have been mistaken, over the years, for the ordinary cost of doing business. Untangling that is slow and unglamorous work, and it tends to yield recommendations that look modest in isolation and, followed steadily, prove worth a good deal more than they seemed.
A representative engagement

By way of illustration rather than inventory, our work this year with {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}} is representative both of the kind of question clients bring us and of the way we prefer to answer it. We offer it as one example of the practice and not as an account of it, and a prospective client who wanted to understand how we work would learn more from that single relationship than from any longer list we might assemble.
The people you would work with

The firm is led by Laura Brown, its Managing Partner, and though this overview is written in the firm's collective voice I will step out of it briefly to say that the register described above is one I hold the practice to personally, in review, where I am at my most exacting with our own overstatements. Working alongside is Richard Marsh, our Engagement Manager, who is the colleague a client is most likely to deal with from one week to the next; he keeps the work moving, he is the one who turns a client's printed, signed, and scanned paperwork into something a team can actually reason from, and he is careful to a fault about using full names and titles wherever the relationship calls for them.

We are deliberately a small firm, and we mean to remain one that a client can reach without first passing through three layers of people who were not in the room. If the questions set out above are the ones keeping a board or a general counsel awake at night, they are the questions this practice was assembled to answer, and we would be glad of the conversation.
Joining the Firm: Barbara Freeman

It is a real pleasure to welcome Barbara Freeman to Verdant Health Advisory, where she joins the Advisory practice as an Analyst, and I am glad to be the one to set the particulars down, because she is very much the sort of colleague we had been hoping to find. Her reporting line runs to Susan Clark, our Principal, who will set her assignments and review her work, and Barbara should regard Susan as her first point of call on anything that touches the substance of an engagement, from the way a finding is framed to the harder question of whether a given conclusion has the evidence behind it to be stated at all.

The role will suit her, I think, precisely because the Analyst's work here rewards the habits she is already known for. We ask our analysts to let a clean and well-ordered table carry the argument and to write sparingly around it, findings first and nothing decorative, and Barbara's instinct for handing back a messy data pull sorted, footnoted, and quietly defensible is exactly the instinct this practice runs on. She will work across our service line, compensation, and revenue cycle engagements as the assignments require, and she will find before long that the analytical spine of all three is a good deal more alike than their subject matter would ever suggest.

The first several weeks will lean toward orientation rather than output, and that is by design. A great deal of what we produce is read by a general counsel before anyone acts on it, so our analysts learn early to draft to that standard, keeping findings and recommendations plainly apart and claiming only what the data will bear, and Susan will take Barbara through a live engagement or two so that the standard becomes something she watches in practice rather than only reads about in a memo. Her workspace, her access to the client shares, and the several accounts she will need are being arranged this week, and anything found to be missing should go straight to Susan so that it is put right at once rather than quietly worked around for a month.

We are fortunate to have her, and I have little doubt the practice will be the better for it. Barbara, welcome; please make yourself known to any of us in these first days, since everyone here still remembers being new, and a firm this small never leaves anyone new for long, and the door of every office here, mine included, is genuinely open while she finds her feet.
Laura Brown, Managing Partner
Welcome to the Practice: Joshua Dougherty

We are glad to welcome Joshua Dougherty to Verdant Health Advisory as an Analyst in the Advisory practice, and I want to set the essentials down here so that his first weeks are as clear to him as they are to the rest of us. His reporting line runs to Susan Clark, our Principal, who will assign and review his work, and Joshua should take any question about the substance of an engagement to Susan first, particularly in these early months when the right answer is not yet obvious to him and no question is too small to bring.

He arrives quick and genuinely eager, which is a fine way to arrive, and the single adjustment he will make in his first stretch here has less to do with ability than with register. We tend to draft toward the shortest version the evidence will fully support, and a newer hand almost always writes past that line at first and then trims back under review; Joshua should expect his early drafts to come back shorter than he sent them, and should read the trimming as the ordinary way this firm arrives at what it is prepared to say, and not as any judgment on the work. The register our readers expect is quieter than instinct suggests, and it is learned by doing far more than by being told.

One discipline is worth naming on the very first day, because so much of what we write is read by a general counsel before anyone acts on it. A recommendation is labelled a recommendation and kept plainly apart from the findings that do or do not support it, and it is never dressed up as a finding to lend it weight it has not earned. Joshua already has the instinct for that distinction, which is part of why we were glad to make the offer, and Susan will reinforce it on live work so that the habit is settled long before it is ever tested on an engagement where the difference carries real consequence.

The practical side is in hand. His workspace, his access to the client shares, and the accounts he will need are being set up this week, and anything found missing should go to Susan so that it is put right at once rather than quietly worked around for a month. We are pleased he has joined us, and I expect the practice will get a great deal from his energy once it is matched to the measured tone our readers count on. Everyone here was new not so long ago, and in a firm this size the newness wears off quickly. Joshua, welcome.
Laura Brown, Managing Partner
Verdant Health Advisory LLC

Some years into this work, the description of the firm we would give a prospective client has not changed a great deal, which is either a want of imagination or a sign that we chose the right ground to stand on. We are a small healthcare advisory practice, and our engagements sit in the unshowy middle of hospital and physician-group operations: whether a service line is earning its place, whether a compensation arrangement would hold up under a fair-market-value review, and where the revenue cycle is losing money that nobody meant to give away.
What has not changed

The discipline is the same as it was when we opened. A general counsel reads a good deal of what we write before anyone acts on it, so we do not assert a conclusion the analysis will not carry, we keep findings ahead of recommendations and label each for what it is, and we use the vocabulary of fair market value carefully, as a term of art with consequences and never as decoration. Clients who have worked with us for a while tell us that this is the part they came to rely on, and it is certainly the part we are least willing to relax.
The work itself

Service line economics remain the most common reason a health system calls, because a hospital nearly always understands its margin in the aggregate far better than it understands the margin of any one department, and the honest allocation of shared cost is where most of the disagreement, and most of the value, actually lives. Physician compensation is the most sensitive of our engagements, since a question about fair market value reaches well past the spreadsheet and into arrangements a client has often already signed. The revenue cycle is the quietest of the three, a matter of many small recoveries rather than one large one, and it rewards the sort of patience that does not photograph well.

The clients we work for tend to be of three broad kinds, and the work looks a little different for each of them. A regional health system carries the weight of scale and a board that reads carefully; an independent physician group feels every finding personally, because the numbers are, in a real sense, its partners' own; and an ambulatory surgery joint venture answers to two or more owners whose interests do not always point the same way, so a finding written for it has to survive being read by parties who would each prefer a different answer. We have learned to write for all three audiences at once, which turns out to be mostly a matter of saying only what is true and saying it in the same words to everyone.
A few engagements, by way of example

It is easier to describe the practice through the work than through adjectives, so, offered as illustration and not as a ledger of everything we do, our engagements with {{fact:f:E-2020-001.client}}, {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}, and {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} are fair examples of the questions clients bring us and of the register in which we answer them. Each is representative rather than exhaustive, and any one of them would tell a prospective client more about how we actually work than a longer roll of names ever could.
How we are built

The firm is led by Laura Brown, its Managing Partner, and it is deliberately small, close enough to the work that a client's difficult question reaches a partner without first being handed down a chain. That size is a choice and not a phase we are impatient to grow out of, because it lets the people who wrote a finding be the same people who sit in the room and defend it, and that is the only arrangement we have found that reliably keeps the writing honest. Growth, when it comes, will be weighed against that property first, since a firm that outgrows it stops being the firm a general counsel learned to trust.
If you are considering us

The clients who get the most from us tend to arrive with a question that has become genuinely uncomfortable, one they need answered in a way they can defend rather than merely repeated back to them in a way that soothes. If that is the position a board or a general counsel finds itself in, it is close to the position this practice was assembled for, and we would welcome the chance to talk it through.
